slides.headline: Amazon Wants Patrolling Cameras. Its Privacy Promise Has Conditions.
slides.subheadline: Inside the prices, flight limits, interior mapping and encryption trade-offs behind Ring’s mobile security pitch.

items.title: Your rooms become a floor plan
items.body: AI Pilot combines cameras, sensors and cloud processing to map interiors and suggest patrol points.

items.title: Scheduling costs beyond the hardware
items.body: Scheduled drone patrols require a compatible Ring Protect plan.

items.title: Up to 8 minutes, not continuous coverage
items.body: Tested with a new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions; actual flight time depends on usage and environment.

slides.headline: One Flies Through Homes. One Patrols Businesses.

left.title: Airborne checks, then back to dock
left.description: 2K video, 148° field of view, 360° rotation and two LED lights; camera off while docked.

right.title: A mobile business security camera
right.description: Streams and records in up to 4K while patrolling; performs a 360° scan at designated stops.

slides.headline: The Price Tags—and the Storage Window

metrics.label: DRONE CAM
metrics.context: Target shipping: January 27, 2027. FCC authorization remains required before sale.

metrics.label: ROVER CAM
metrics.context: Preorders open; U.S. shipping scheduled for December 16, 2026.

metrics.label: MAXIMUM CLOUD VIDEO HISTORY
metrics.context: Up to this limit for doorbell rings, motion events and Live View events; compatible subscription required.

slides.context: Both robots use Throw Away the Key encryption. EFF says it falls short of end-to-end protection.

slides.headline: Throwing Away Keys Does Not End Access

items.title: Ring gets a processing window
items.body: TAKE permits cloud processing before Ring deletes its key copies after 24 hours.

items.title: Playback can reopen that window
items.body: Watching older footage or using smart features can send keys back to Ring’s servers.

items.title: An improvement, not end-to-end encryption
items.body: EFF credits stronger defaults but says genuine end-to-end encryption prevents the provider from ever accessing keys.

slides.headline: Visible Recording Is Not Complete Privacy

left.title: If recording is obvious, privacy is solved
left.description: Amazon emphasizes LED recording indicators, audible drone propellers and Rover’s visible light tower.

right.title: Indicators reveal activity—not data access
right.description: Cloud mapping and temporary decryption remain separate questions that visible recording signals cannot resolve.​

slides.headline: Privacy-First Homes: Hold Off. Businesses: Audit First.

avoid.title: Households prioritizing minimal indoor surveillance
points: Hold off if interior mapping and cloud processing exceed your privacy boundaries.
Do not mistake an up-to-8-minute flight for continuous airborne coverage.

fit.title: Businesses with compatible single-floor premises
points: Claimed coverage: up to 5,000 square feet; indoor, single-floor operation only, with no stair climbing.​
Exclude curved edges, sunken areas, black glossy floors and transitions greater than 1.375"/3.5cm.

slides.headline: Before Patrols Expand, Set the Rules

items.title: Define where cameras may travel
items.body: Approve routes, recording hours and restricted rooms before enabling automated patrols.

items.title: Choose a storage window deliberately
items.body: Set retention around actual security needs, not the longest available history.

items.title: Review recording policies before deployment
items.body: Decide who can view footage, how occupants receive notice and what evidence would justify expanding coverage.

slides.headline: A Moving Camera Needs More Than a Privacy Promise
slides.verdict: Privacy-first households should wait. Businesses should validate navigation, recording policies, retention and access before buying.
slides.question: Would you let a security camera map and patrol your private rooms?
slides.actionText: Where do you draw the line?
